title: Impact of Generative AI-assisted programming on the computational thinking of high school students
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether Generative AI-assisted programming improves high school students’ computational thinking, and whether its effects differ across sub-skills. The authors note that most prior work on ChatGPT-like support has focused on higher education, while K-12 evidence—especially on fine-grained computational thinking dimensions—is limited. They frame Generative AI as a potential scaffolding tool that can reduce syntactic burden, support debugging, and free students’ cognitive resources for higher-order problem solving.

The study was conducted with 83 tenth-grade students at one high school in western China. Using a convergent parallel mixed-methods quasi-experimental design, one intact class was assigned to the Generative AI-assisted condition and another to teacher-led instruction. The intervention lasted 8 weeks and used iFlytek Spark to help students learn Python syntax, understand code, and debug programs during programming projects. Quantitative data came from pre/post computational thinking tests based on the Bebras CT Challenge, and qualitative data came from semi-structured interviews with 18 students.

Results showed that the Generative AI group improved significantly more than the control group on overall computational thinking, algorithmic modeling, and abstraction/decomposition, but not on pattern recognition and evaluation. Interview data suggested that students valued the AI for personalized support, immediate feedback, code explanation, and efficiency, but some worried about over-dependence and occasionally unclear answers. The authors conclude that Generative AI can be an effective scaffold for high school programming instruction, though its benefits may vary by computational thinking dimension and require careful classroom guidance to avoid dependency.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental mixed-methods study with a comparison group, pretest-posttest design, and clearly reported quantitative analyses, but it lacks random assignment at the individual level and is limited to one school. Those design constraints keep it below blue, though it is stronger than a purely qualitative or correlational study.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports medium-to-large effects on a priority population: high school students learning programming, with partial η² values of 0.120 to 0.216 for key computational thinking subskills. The impact is meaningfully positive overall, despite one null subscale result.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI-assisted programming support using iFlytek Spark (ChatGPT-like conversational AI) to explain Python code, answer syntax questions, generate examples, and provide debugging help during middle/high school programming lessons.

finding.finding_summary: Generative AI-assisted programming produced significant gains in overall computational thinking for the experimental group (n=42) compared with teacher-led instruction (n=41). The repeated-measures ANOVA showed a significant method-by-time interaction, F(1,81)=14.29, p<0.001, partial η²=0.150, indicating a large effect on computational thinking as measured by the Bebras CT Challenge.
finding.measure: Bebras CT Challenge overall computational thinking score

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was especially effective for algorithmic modeling. The experimental group improved from M=17.17 to 21.38, while the control group changed from M=17.78 to 17.80; the method-by-time interaction was significant, F(1,81)=22.315, p<0.001, partial η²=0.216, a large effect. This suggests the conversational AI mainly supported structured problem solving and algorithm design.
finding.measure: Bebras CT Challenge algorithmic modeling subscale

finding.finding_summary: For abstraction and decomposition, the experimental group improved from M=13.76 to 22.43, compared with the control group’s increase from M=13.89 to 18.13. The interaction was significant, F(1,81)=11.065, p=0.001, partial η²=0.120, indicating a medium effect favoring Generative AI-assisted learning.
finding.measure: Bebras CT Challenge abstraction and decomposition subscale

finding.finding_summary: Pattern recognition and evaluation did not show a statistically reliable advantage for Generative AI after Bonferroni correction. The interaction was F(1,81)=5.194, p=0.025, partial η²=0.060, but this did not meet the corrected alpha of 0.0125; the experimental group showed a slight non-significant decline (M=-0.26) while the control group improved significantly (M=1.59).
finding.measure: Bebras CT Challenge pattern recognition and evaluation subscale

finding.finding_summary: Interview data indicated that students perceived the AI as increasing initiative, motivation, and willingness to ask questions. Students emphasized individualized support, ease of use, and rapid responses as reasons they felt more engaged and less intimidated by programming; these are qualitative findings from 18 interviewed students rather than a separate quantified outcome.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on learning initiative, engagement, and perceived motivation
